articles.title: The most ambitious ideas to save the world from El Niño
articles.summary: A monster El Niño is brewing in the Pacific Ocean – but there may be ways we can stop the worst impacts from occurring
articles.content:
A monster El Niño is brewing in the Pacific Ocean – but there may be ways we can stop the worst impacts from occurring

Flood defences, like this one in California, are just one way to protect communities from El Niño Mario Tama/Getty Images

Countries around the world are bracing for a torrid few months as the El Niño weather phenomenon looks set to wreak havoc on shorelines, farmland and ocean ecosystems.

Already, India is grappling with the impacts of one of the driest monsoon seasons on record. Meanwhile, in Indonesia, schools have closed and authorities have advised residents to stay indoors to avoid the toxic smoke from huge wildfires supercharged by El Niño.

But what if we could take the sting out of the tail of El Niño – or even stop it from happening altogether? That’s the hope of physicists, chemists and engineers working on ideas ranging from the outrageously radical to the just-might-work.

Advertisement

One of the most ambitious ideas for halting El Niño is to repurpose a technique called artificial upwelling that was initially conceived to boost the uptake of carbon by the oceans. This form of geoengineering involves pumping cold, nutrient-rich water from the deep ocean up to the surface to encourage the growth of plankton, which would then absorb and store carbon from the atmosphere.

Katharine Ricke at the University of California, San Diego, says artificial upwelling could be used to cool sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific, potentially preventing an El Niño from forming.

But – and it is a big but – the technical feasibility of deploying artificial upwelling on this scale would be a “major, major undertaking”, she says. Ricke has previously investigated whether the approach could be used to cool sea-surface temperatures in the Indian Ocean and found it would require approximately 5.8 million kilometres of pipe, nearly double the total length of all pipelines in the world.

There is also the problem that nobody knows what putting that amount of pipework into the ocean would do to other marine life. “The ecosystem effects of installing ocean pipes at that scale are really not well understood at all,” she says.

Another equally ambitious, but perhaps more promising, approach for preventing El Niño could be to use another geoengineering technique called marine cloud brightening.

The El Niño climate phase occurs when easterly winds weaken, allowing warm water built up in the western Pacific to slosh back across the central and eastern parts of the ocean. Spraying droplets of seawater into the air below low-lying stratocumulus clouds in the Pacific would increase their brightness, reflecting more sunlight back to space. This would then bring down sea-surface temperatures, strengthening trade winds to blow warm water back into the western Pacific and reverse the El Niño pattern.

A study published in July, co-authored by Ricke, concluded that deploying marine cloud brightening in this way would dramatically reduce the strength of an El Niño and push the system back into a neutral state much earlier than normal.

This won’t come in time to prevent the current El Niño, says Jessica Wan at the University of Chicago, a co-author of the research. The technology needed to brighten clouds on this scale doesn’t exist, plus there is no international framework for countries to agree this kind of geoengineering intervention. “It’s not something we could implement for this El Niño or maybe even the next one,” says Wan.

So, for now at least, El Niño cycles aren’t going anywhere – but can we make them more tolerable?

One particularly devastating consequence of the way El Niño turns up the global temperature dial and shifts rain patterns around the world is that it threatens food supplies. The United Nations World Food Programme estimates that 274 million people in 45 countries will be acutely food insecure by the end of 2027, 49 million more than today.

In hot water

Work is under way to develop new breeds of crops capable of withstanding the extreme conditions brought about with El Niño. Rice is a particular priority, says Erik Murchie at the University of Nottingham in the UK.

Murchie is part of a team developing heat-tolerant rice varieties, with trials now ongoing in the Philippines. This is part of a global effort: in 2025, researchers in China reported the discovery of a gene variant that can preserve yield and rice quality during hot nights, one of the major threats to rice yields. Gene-editing or selective breeding could allow this trait in commercial crops, the team says, with the field trials indicating a 31 to 78 per cent greater yield under high temperatures compared with standard rice strains.

Such a goal isn’t a fantasy – in the 1990s, scientists pinpointed a rice gene that allows a traditional rice variety known as FR13A to survive a week of submergence in flood water. The SUB1 gene has since been introduced into several major rice varieties around the world, making crops more resilient to climate-driven flood risks.

Housing, people and infrastructure are also vulnerable to rising water levels and flooding driven by El Niño. Traditional flood-protection measures are already being deployed, from coastal barricades to temporary barriers. In California, drains are being cleared and sandbags handed out, while residents are being urged to prepare their properties for high winds and flood risk.

But one company has a more drastic idea to protect against flood risk more permanently: raising the height of land. California start-up Terranova has developed a robot that injects a mix of wood slurry into the ground, raising the height of land at risk of flooding from sea-level rise.

The robots drill wells around 12 to 18 metres deep into the ground and then inject the mix, made from wood waste, into the earth. The robotic system can lift up a roughly 4000-square-metre area by about 30 centimetres per day, the firm says. “We’re combining heavy robotics and geotechnical innovation to literally reshape the world,” the firm’s CEO Laurence Allen said in a 2025 statement announcing $7 million of venture capital investment.

However, Nigel Wright at the University of Birmingham in the UK says extensive testing should be done before deploying the technology at a large scale. He queries whether the wood waste would solidify, remain as slurry or decompose underground over the long term. “I would question whether the soil structure would be stable enough over 20 or 30 years to actually support houses,” he says.

Hexagonal floating shades are being tested to protect coral reefs University of Miami

Inside the oceans, coral reefs are on the front line of the El Niño crisis. Elevated ocean temperatures caused by El Niño can cause mass coral-bleaching events, in which corals expel the symbiotic algae living in their tissues. This process can severely stress, and ultimately kill, corals.

Shading corals could help. One test of the approach is happening this month: five floating hexagons that block harmful ultraviolet rays are being installed in a small coral nursery in Florida. The plan is to extend this to 100 shading units in June next year, which will be distributed among restoration organisations working across Florida to test their effectiveness at protecting corals and any impact on the long-term health of the ecosystem.

In Australia, an approach that goes even further has been tested. Greg Qiao at the University of Melbourne set out more than a decade ago to create a chemical film that would sit atop agricultural reservoirs to minimise water loss to evaporation. After extensive trials, that idea never came to fruition – but Qiao realised the work could be repurposed for coral reefs.

The aim for a coral reef is to block sunlight, rather than prevent evaporation, so Qiao’s team developed a thin film layer made from calcium carbonate coated with stearic acid. The layer is one molecule thick and designed to sit on the surface of the ocean above a reef. Field trials in 2018 suggested the film reduced light hitting the corals by 30 per cent. “That’s probably enough for us to stop the bleach,” says Qiao. The film would maybe last for only a few hours before dissipating, but that might be enough to offer protection for corals during a period of peak bleaching risk, he says.

Just like with many of the protection efforts against El Niño, coral shading is still in its infancy. There are promising signs that we may one day have a future without such dramatic global swings, but, for now, El Niño is here to stay.
articles.reasoning: The article discusses ambitious, innovative geoengineering and agricultural strategies to mitigate the severe environmental and societal impacts of El Niño, including cooling ocean temperatures, protecting coral reefs, and developing heat-tolerant crops. These efforts represent significant, hopeful advances with broad potential benefits for global food security, ecosystem preservation, and climate resilience.
articles.personality_title: New ideas aim to reduce the harm caused by El Niño
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – El Niño is a weather pattern that happens in the Pacific Ocean and can cause serious problems like floods, droughts, and damage to coral reefs. This year, a strong El Niño is expected to cause trouble in many parts of the world.

**What happened** – Scientists and engineers are working on bold new methods to lessen the effects of El Niño. Some ideas include pumping cold water from deep in the ocean to cool the surface, making clouds brighter to reflect sunlight, creating heat-resistant rice, raising land using robots to prevent flooding, and shading coral reefs to protect them from heat.

**Impact** – These ideas could help protect food supplies, homes, and ocean life from the damage El Niño causes. For example, heat-tolerant rice can grow better during hot weather, and shading coral reefs might stop them from dying. Although some projects are still being tested and need more research, they show new ways to help communities and nature cope with climate challenges.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue testing these technologies to understand their safety and effectiveness. Some, like cloud brightening and land-raising robots, need more development before they can be used widely. Meanwhile, farmers and governments are preparing by adopting stronger crops and building flood defenses.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists are exploring several innovative methods to reduce El Niño’s damage, aiming to protect people, crops, and oceans from its harmful effects.
articles.personality_title_fr: De nouvelles idées pour réduire les dégâts causés par El Niño
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – El Niño est un phénomène météorologique dans l’océan Pacifique qui peut causer de graves problèmes comme des inondations, des sécheresses et des dégâts aux récifs coralliens. Cette année, un fort El Niño est attendu et devrait provoquer des troubles dans de nombreuses régions du monde.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques et ingénieurs développent des méthodes audacieuses pour diminuer les effets d’El Niño. Parmi elles, pomper de l’eau froide des profondeurs pour refroidir la surface, rendre les nuages plus brillants pour réfléchir le soleil, créer du riz résistant à la chaleur, élever les terres avec des robots pour éviter les inondations, et protéger les coraux par de l’ombre.

**Impact** – Ces idées pourraient protéger les récoltes, les maisons et la vie marine des dégâts provoqués par El Niño. Par exemple, le riz résistant à la chaleur pousse mieux par temps chaud, et l’ombre sur les coraux pourrait éviter leur mort. Même si certains projets sont encore en phase d’essai et nécessitent plus de recherches, ils ouvrent de nouvelles voies pour aider les communautés et la nature face au changement climatique.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à tester ces technologies pour vérifier leur sécurité et leur efficacité. Certaines, comme l’éclaircissement des nuages et les robots d’élévation des sols, demandent encore du développement avant un usage large. En attendant, agriculteurs et gouvernements se préparent avec des cultures renforcées et des protections contre les inondations.

articles.personality_title_es: Nuevas ideas para reducir los daños causados por El Niño
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El Niño es un fenómeno climático en el Océano Pacífico que puede causar problemas graves como inundaciones, sequías y daños a los arrecifes de coral. Este año se espera un El Niño fuerte que podría afectar a muchas partes del mundo.

Mientras tanto, agricultores y gobiernos se preparan con cultivos más fuertes y defensas contra inundaciones.

articles.title: The Great Plains face a surprising threat: Too many trees
articles.content:
This story was produced by Grist and co-published with the Nebraska Examiner

To really understand what’s going on in the Nebraska Sandhills, Shelly Kelly told me, it’s helpful to see it from the air. From the window of her father’s Bonanza A36, we looked out over the heart of one of the most rural landscapes in the United States. The Sandhills are a 19,500 square-mile swath of grassy dunes embellished with grazing cattle, serpentine rivers, and sunflowers.

Kelly has spent her life on the prairies of the High Plains. As a child, she made bouquets of flowering grasses and hunted for mudpuppies in the interdunal buffalo wallows on her parents’ ranch. Now a rancher herself, she’s trying to preserve the landscape she loves against the usual suspects — overgrazing and overharvesting — and one surprising new threat: trees.

She pointed out my window to the prairie below. “You can see it there,” she said, pointing to a neat grove of Juniperus virginiana, eastern red cedar, deliberately planted by ranchers to protect calving heifers from the wind. These windbreaks are standard features on the Plains. But to the south of their orderly rows, a dozen cedars have popped up in the middle of the grass, scattering across the nearby range like race-runners breaking free of the pack.

This spreading of trees is known as woody encroachment — or the “green glacier,” as some call it, evoking the slow creep of tree species over grasslands — and it’s got ecologists and ranchers of the Plains on high alert.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“We’re losing our biodiversity,” Kelly said. “We’re losing our resiliency.”

Trees grow along the Spring Creek Prairie Audubon Center in March 2024 near Lincoln, Nebraska. The Center works to conserve the tallgrass prairie ecosystem and associated wildlife.

David Madison / Getty Images

For ranchers, a woody takeover of their rangeland creates an obvious problem: less land to graze. The Texas A&M Agrilife extension estimates that woody encroachment over the 10 Great Plains states represents $4 billion in lost range production. Ecologists predict biodiversity losses would affect the insects, birds, and small mammals that populate the country’s remaining prairies. Everybody worries about what those thirsty trees will do to the already stressed water supply as the green glacier expands from the wetter climate in the eastern prairie states to the arid western regions.

Prairies — on the High Plains and around the world — thrive in cycles of stability and disruption. Fire, grazing, dry seasons, and the area’s particular mix of vegetation all play a role in preserving the healthy root systems that allow a diverse mix of grasses to continue growing year after year. Some heartier grasses with root systems 20 feet deep can keep the prairie green in a drought, while healthy soil can hold dormant seeds until the conditions are right.

Fire — both naturally-occurring and prescribed burns — has long been a feature of the prairie landscape. Suppressing it is part of what has allowed woody plants to seed, spread, and develop the thick bark that makes them more likely to then withstand future fires. Meanwhile, overgrazing reduces trees’ and shrubs’ grassy competition, allowing them to grow faster. Cattle and bison don’t eat the woody plants. Goats, sheep, elk, and other “browsing” species don’t eat enough of them to control the spread, though some are experimenting with browsers as a component of a larger management plan.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The Flint Hills of Kansas and Osage Hills of Oklahoma are home to two-thirds of the nation’s remaining tallgrass prairie, said Brian Obermeyer, The Nature Conservancy’s Great Plains grasslands strategy director. The persistence of the prairie in this region is largely because of the longstanding culture of prescribed burns, dating back to when Chisholm Trail cattle drives would divert their skinnier livestock to fatten up on the highly nutritious, tender, juicy grasses that grow back after a burn. Obermeyer even found a lease contract dating back to 1915 requiring the land to be burned regularly so that cattle would have access to the new growth. But in regions where that practice is not common, Obermeyer said, “Getting people comfortable with the culture of prescribed fire takes time.”

The Sandhills in Nebraska don’t have the fire culture, though Kelly and others are trying to change that. What they do have, Kelly said, is a culture of tree-planting.

“Most of the people that settled Nebraska came from areas that were full of trees,” she said. In fact, before it was known as the “Cornhusker State,” Nebraska’s official nickname was the “Tree Planter State.” It dates back to the Homestead Act of 1862, which required settlers to cultivate their land with crops or trees to establish ownership, and Nebraska’s Kinkaid Act of 1904, which offered free trees to help settlers cultivate 640-acre tracts in the state. The tradition has gone on for centuries now, and thanks to advances in horticulture, ranchers buy heartier and heartier red cedar saplings for their windbreaks, which then spread their juggernaut offspring across the plains.

As executive director of the Sandhills Task Force, a nonprofit established 33 years ago to promote conservation and sustainable land management in the ranching industry, Kelly knows that half the battle is changing the culture. “We’re not talking about trees being bad everywhere,” she said. “But trees are not good on a prairie, especially invasive trees.” On her water bottle I spotted a sticker: Be A Leader, Cut a Cedar.

Another cultural shift might be necessary as well, particularly for the broader conservation community. The prevailing climate wisdom has been pretty clear: Trees are good, and planting them is virtuous — the more the better. But actually, Obermeyer said, grasslands can be a more secure carbon sink than forests. A big reason for that goes back to the cycle of fire on the landscape, and the worsening threat of out-of-control wildfires that are often the result of too much fire suppression. Woody plants store most of their carbon above ground in their trunks and leaves. When they burn, all of that carbon is released, and the charred remains continue to release carbon after the initial burn. It can take years for the forest to return to its storage capacity. Grasslands store the vast majority of carbon safely underground in their deep root systems, and after a fire their stems and blades quickly rebound.

The sun rises over the Joseph H. Williams Tallgrass Prairie Preserve in Osage County in June 2026 in Pawhuska, Oklahoma.

Heather Diehl / Getty Images

There is evidence that the increased atmospheric carbon may be giving another advantage to woody plants, which utilize a different carbon pathway than grasses in photosynthesis, making them more efficient photosynthesizers in carbon-soaked, warm, dry air. While this means that trees may, in the short term, capture carbon more quickly, the loss of an entire ecosystem, especially one that stores carbon more securely, isn’t a good tradeoff in the long term, said Chris Helzer, Nebraska director of science and stewardship for The Nature Conservancy.

Climate change is one of many reasons that a non-intervention strategy — letting nature take its course — won’t work on the High Plains. There are too many things in motion to simply go “hands-off.” But, really, Helzer said, grasslands as we know them have never been free of human intervention. From the time that Indigenous peoples hunted free-ranging bison, grasslands have evolved in tandem with humans, explained Helzer. The Nature Conservancy has also worked with the InterTribal Buffalo Council and Tanka Fund to support the return of bison to the Plains along with other tribal-led efforts to restore damaged ecosystems and build management capacity.

Ranchers also have a critical role to play, Helzer said. And many are playing it with gusto. Kelly’s dad, John Taylor, has had a front-row seat to his daughter’s crusade and benefited from her growing expertise. On his ranch the cedar is under control, but near the fenceline, a few of the evergreen treetops peeked over a neighboring dune, like Birnam Wood advancing on MacBeth’s Dunsinane Hill. These trees are prolific, spreading their seeds across a 200-foot radius. Seedlings grow at about a rate of 1 to 2 feet per year, and once they reach 5 feet tall, they start spreading seed in their own 200-foot radius. That said, the Sandhills are mostly lucky, Kelly said. Eastern red cedar is easy to kill. Cut it down to the root and it mostly doesn’t grow back.

A red cedar grows near Wauneta, Nebraska. Getty Images Over 2,000 bison, also known as American buffalo, roam in the Joseph H. Williams Tallgrass Prairie Preserve in Osage County in June 2026 in Pawhuska, Oklahoma. Heather Diehl / Getty Images

Kelly has even helped Nebraskans connect to funding opportunities to clear the cedars. Through grants and fundraising, the Sandhills Task Force can help ranchers pay for up to 75 percent of cedar removal. The funds are stimulating a growing cedar removal industry in the region. State and federal programs will also help fund the removal — but, ironically, the same departments still subsidize tree-planting for windbreaks, Kelly said, though they are increasingly discouraging red cedars.

The Nature Conservancy is using its preserves to test grazing patterns, new mixes of plant species, and other mitigation techniques that can help private landowners across the High Plains find the right balance of grazing, burning, and rewilding to keep their grasslands healthy. “To some extent, you can have a prairie that has trees,” Helzer said. “But there’s a line — when you cross that line, you have a woodland with clearings, not a grassland with trees.”

Grassland prairies — short, mixed, tall, and other types — used to stretch from Texas to the Dakotas, into Kentucky and up to the foothills of the Rockies. Only 4 percent of tallgrass prairies are left, making it, Obermeyer said, “the most altered landscape in North America in terms of acres lost.” At the same time, he said, places like the Flint Hills and Sandhills give him hope. More people are recognizing the subtle beauty and ecological power of the plains. “We can’t lose sight of the fact that we have a tremendous amount that we have the chance to preserve,” Obermeyer said. “We have a lot of opportunities to get this right.”
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant ecological challenge—woody encroachment threatening the Great Plains grasslands—but also details ongoing conservation efforts, cultural shifts, and scientific strategies to preserve and restore this vital ecosystem. It emphasizes broad environmental impact, the importance of prairie preservation for biodiversity and carbon storage, and community and organizational actions to address the issue, providing substantial context and hopeful prospects.
articles.personality_title: Great Plains fight back as trees spread into grasslands
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Great Plains, known for their wide open grasslands and cattle ranches, face a new challenge. Trees, especially eastern red cedars, are growing where mostly grasses used to thrive. This process, called woody encroachment, is changing the landscape and affecting wildlife and farming.

**What happened** – In Nebraska’s Sandhills, ranchers like Shelly Kelly have noticed more cedar trees spreading beyond the windbreaks they planted. These trees grow quickly and take over grazing land. Fire suppression and grazing habits have helped these trees spread, because fires that once kept them in check are less common. Ranchers and conservation groups are now working together to remove these trees and bring back the prairie.

**Impact** – The growing number of trees means less space for cattle to graze and threatens the insects, birds, and animals that live in the grasslands. Trees also use more water, which is a problem in this dry region. Grasslands store carbon underground, helping fight climate change, while trees store it above ground and release it when they burn. Losing grasslands could reduce this natural carbon storage.

**What's next step** – Groups like The Nature Conservancy and the Sandhills Task Force are encouraging controlled fires, better grazing plans, and removing cedar trees. They offer financial help to ranchers to clear trees and promote a culture that values prairie preservation. Scientists are also testing new ways to keep the grasslands healthy.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Ranchers and conservationists are joining forces to stop spreading trees from taking over the Great Plains, protecting grasslands that support wildlife, farming, and climate health.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les Grandes Plaines luttent contre l’envahissement des arbres dans les prairies
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les Grandes Plaines, célèbres pour leurs vastes prairies et leurs ranchs de bétail, font face à un nouveau défi. Des arbres, surtout des cèdres rouges de l’Est, poussent là où il y avait principalement de l’herbe. Ce phénomène, appelé encroachment ligneux, transforme le paysage et affecte la faune et l’agriculture.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Dans les dunes de sable du Nebraska, des éleveurs comme Shelly Kelly ont vu de plus en plus de cèdres s’étendre au-delà des brise-vent qu’ils avaient plantés. Ces arbres poussent vite et prennent la place des pâturages. La suppression des incendies et les habitudes de pâturage ont aidé ces arbres à se répandre, car les feux qui les contrôlaient sont moins fréquents. Éleveurs et groupes de conservation travaillent maintenant ensemble pour enlever ces arbres et restaurer la prairie.

**Impact** – L’augmentation des arbres réduit l’espace pour le bétail et menace les insectes, oiseaux, et animaux qui vivent dans les prairies. Les arbres consomment aussi plus d’eau, un problème dans cette région sèche. Les prairies stockent le carbone sous terre, aidant à lutter contre le changement climatique, tandis que les arbres le stockent au-dessus du sol et le libèrent en brûlant. Perdre les prairies pourrait réduire ce stockage naturel de carbone.

**Prochaine étape** – Des organisations comme The Nature Conservancy et le Sandhills Task Force encouragent les brûlages contrôlés, de meilleures pratiques de pâturage, et l’élimination des cèdres. Elles aident financièrement les éleveurs à enlever les arbres et favorisent une culture qui valorise la préservation des prairies. Des scientifiques testent aussi de nouvelles méthodes pour garder les prairies en bonne santé.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Éleveurs et écologistes unissent leurs efforts pour stopper l’envahissement des arbres dans les Grandes Plaines, protégeant des prairies essentielles à la faune, à l’agriculture et au climat.
articles.personality_title_es: Las Grandes Llanuras luchan para frenar la expansión de árboles en las praderas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las Grandes Llanuras, conocidas por sus extensas praderas y ranchos de ganado, enfrentan un nuevo problema. Árboles, especialmente cedros rojos del este, están creciendo donde antes solo había pastos. Este proceso, llamado invasión leñosa, está cambiando el paisaje y afectando a la vida silvestre y la agricultura.

**Qué pasó** – En las dunas de arena de Nebraska, rancheros como Shelly Kelly han notado que más cedros se extienden más allá de las barreras de viento que ellos mismos plantaron. Estos árboles crecen rápido y ocupan espacio para el pastoreo. La supresión de incendios y las prácticas de pastoreo han ayudado a que los árboles se propaguen, porque los fuegos que antes los controlaban son menos frecuentes. Ahora rancheros y grupos conservacionistas trabajan juntos para eliminar estos árboles y restaurar la pradera.

**Impacto** – El aumento de árboles significa menos espacio para que el ganado pastoree y amenaza a insectos, aves y animales que viven en las praderas. Los árboles también usan más agua, un problema en esta zona seca. Las praderas almacenan carbono bajo tierra, ayudando a combatir el cambio climático, mientras que los árboles lo almacenan sobre la tierra y lo liberan cuando arden. Perder praderas podría reducir este almacenamiento natural de carbono.

**Próximo paso** – Organizaciones como The Nature Conservancy y Sandhills Task Force promueven quemas controladas, mejores planes de pastoreo y la eliminación de cedros. Ofrecen ayuda económica a rancheros para limpiar árboles y fomentan una cultura que valora la preservación de praderas. Científicos también prueban nuevas formas de mantener las praderas saludables.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Rancheros y conservacionistas unen fuerzas para detener la invasión de árboles en las Grandes Llanuras, protegiendo praderas vitales para la vida silvestre, la agricultura y la salud del clima.

The post 6 things that will bring more birds to your backyard this autumn first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

If you’ve ever caught a flash of movement in the branches in early October – something small and unfamiliar, not the usual backyard regulars – there’s a good chance it was a migrating bird passing through and looking for somewhere to stop. Tens of millions travel through the country every autumn, flying at night and landing wherever they can when their fat reserves run low at dawn. Most yards don’t have much to offer them. A few simple changes can make yours one that does.

Bob Mulvihill, lead ornithologist at the National Aviary, has six specific things you can do this season to make your outdoor space worth stopping at. Some take just a few minutes. Some are about holding off on things you were already planning to do.

Plant trees and shrubs that fruit in fall

If you’re already planning to add something to the yard this season, let the birds weigh in. Native fruiting trees and shrubs give migrating and resident birds exactly what they’re searching for as wild food sources thin out. Mulvihill’s list includes flowering dogwood, pagoda dogwood, elderberry, viburnum, flowering crabapple (small-fruited varieties can pull in Cedar Waxwings by the dozen), holly, spicebush, wild grapes including Virginia creeper, and wild cherry trees.

Many of these are available at nurseries already established, so you can get them in the ground or in a container this week. They don’t just help once; a good native fruiting tree or shrub keeps producing for years, and they tend to become the most active corners of the yard come migration time.

Don’t cut back those spent flowers yet

It’s tempting to tidy everything up in September and October. Hold off. The seed heads on spent flowers are food, and for certain birds they become a central part of the autumn diet as other sources dry up. Goldfinches, juncos, and many kinds of sparrows will return to them repeatedly through fall and into winter.

Mulvihill names a few native wildflowers that are especially productive: joe-pye weed, ironweed, goldenrods, asters, and wild sunflowers. “If you plant a native wildflower garden with joe-pye weed, ironweed, goldenrods, asters, and wild sunflowers,” he says, “you will soon have a five-star songbird restaurant that will get rave reviews.” A patch of these in a back corner, left standing through the cold months, does more for local bird life than most feeders.

Add moving water

A birdbath is fine in summer, but it won’t attract the full range of birds moving through in autumn. Many migrating species, including warblers and vireos, don’t eat seeds or fruit at all, which means water is the only thing that will pull them in. Migrants specifically look for water that’s moving rather than still, and a flat, standing dish is easy to miss.

If you’re not ready to install anything permanent, there are easy DIY options: a dripper or small solar-powered pump in an existing birdbath creates enough movement to make a difference. “A small, natural-looking moving-water feature will catch the eye of our resident birds and any birds that are just passing through on migration,” Mulvihill says. You’ll start seeing visitors that would never show up otherwise.

Build a brush pile

Before your yard waste goes out to the curb, consider keeping some of it. A loose pile of branches, sticks, and garden debris in a back corner becomes habitat almost immediately: cover from predators for sparrows, towhees, blackbirds, and buntings, along with a source of spiders and other invertebrates that birds will actively forage through. “Brush piles give birds excellent cover from predators, at the same time providing lots of nooks and crannies for spiders and other invertebrates that birds will feed on,” Mulvihill says.

It doesn’t need to be large or elaborate. Even a modest pile makes a real difference. Year-round resident Carolina wrens, which tend to stick close to dense cover, will use it constantly and reward you with a song that’s disproportionately loud for such a small bird.

Keep cats inside during migration

This one is harder to hear if you have an outdoor cat. But Mulvihill notes that free-ranging domestic cats kill more than a billion songbirds in the United States every year, and migrating birds are particularly easy targets: they fly through the night and land exhausted at dawn on the first patch of greenery they find, which may be your backyard. An alert cat in that space at that moment is a real problem for a bird running on empty.

Keeping cats indoors during the spring and fall migration peaks, roughly March through May and August through November, helps both the birds and the cats, which are also safer from traffic, predators, and disease when they stay inside.

Make your windows and outdoor lights safer

A couple of changes around the house can reduce risk before birds even reach the yard. Windows are a bigger hazard than most people realize: a bird heading toward a window sees sky or trees reflected back and has no way of knowing glass is there. UV-reflective dot or stripe patterns on the outside of windows facing the yard break up those reflections enough to register as a solid surface. Horizontal strings on the exterior, spaced roughly two inches apart, work just as well and cost almost nothing.

Outdoor lights are a similar issue during migration season. Many birds navigate at night by stars and ambient light, and lit windows and exterior fixtures can disorient them the way a porch light confuses moths. Turning exterior lights off at night or drawing blinds on bright rooms during peak migration months is one of the easier changes on this list, and it helps.

A few native plants, a water feature, a brush pile in the corner, some strings on the windows, lights off at night. It sounds like a lot written out like that, but most of it takes an afternoon. Some of these birds are flying thousands of miles, running on fat reserves they’ve spent weeks building up. Taking all of that into consideration, it makes sense that what you put out for them at dawn truly matters.

articles.personality_title: Six easy ways to welcome more birds to your backyard this autumn
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every autumn, millions of birds travel across the country, stopping in yards as they migrate. Many yards don’t provide the food or shelter these birds need during their long journeys.

**What happened** – Bob Mulvihill, an expert bird scientist, shared six simple actions people can take this fall to make their yards friendlier for migrating and local birds. These include planting native fruiting trees and shrubs, leaving flower seed heads standing, adding moving water, building a brush pile, keeping cats indoors during migration, and making windows and outdoor lights safer for birds.

**Impact** – These steps help tired migrating birds find food, water, and shelter, increasing their chances of survival. For example, native plants provide natural food sources that last for years, and moving water attracts birds that don’t eat seeds. Keeping cats inside reduces the risk of birds being hunted when they are most vulnerable.

**What's next step** – People can start by planting native plants available at local nurseries or setting up simple water features this week. Over time, more yards will become safe resting spots for birds during migration, which may help bird populations stay strong.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Simple changes like planting native plants and providing water can turn any yard into a vital stop for migrating birds this autumn.
articles.personality_title_fr: Six gestes simples pour attirer plus d’oiseaux dans votre jardin cet automne
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Chaque automne, des millions d’oiseaux migrateurs traversent le pays et s’arrêtent dans les jardins. Beaucoup de jardins n’offrent pas la nourriture ou l’abri dont ces oiseaux ont besoin pendant leur long voyage.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Bob Mulvihill, un expert en ornithologie, a partagé six actions faciles à faire cet automne pour rendre les jardins plus accueillants pour les oiseaux migrateurs et locaux. Parmi elles : planter des arbres et arbustes fruitiers indigènes, ne pas couper les fleurs fanées, ajouter de l’eau en mouvement, construire un tas de branches, garder les chats à l’intérieur pendant la migration, et sécuriser les fenêtres et lumières extérieures.

**Impact** – Ces gestes aident les oiseaux fatigués à trouver nourriture, eau et abri, ce qui augmente leurs chances de survie. Par exemple, les plantes indigènes fournissent des fruits naturels pendant plusieurs années, et l’eau en mouvement attire les oiseaux qui ne mangent pas de graines. Garder les chats à l’intérieur réduit les risques de prédation.

**Prochaine étape** – Les gens peuvent commencer par planter des plantes indigènes disponibles en pépinière ou installer une fontaine d’eau simple cette semaine. Avec le temps, plus de jardins deviendront des haltes sûres pour les oiseaux en migration, ce qui peut aider à préserver leurs populations.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des changements simples comme planter des plantes indigènes et offrir de l’eau peuvent transformer un jardin en une halte essentielle pour les oiseaux migrateurs cet automne.
articles.personality_title_es: Seis formas fáciles de atraer más aves a tu jardín este otoño
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada otoño, millones de aves migratorias cruzan el país y hacen paradas en jardines. Muchos jardines no ofrecen la comida o el refugio que estas aves necesitan durante su largo viaje.

**Qué pasó** – Bob Mulvihill, un experto en aves, compartió seis acciones sencillas que las personas pueden hacer este otoño para que sus jardines sean más amigables para las aves migratorias y residentes. Estas incluyen plantar árboles y arbustos nativos que dan frutos, dejar las flores secas, añadir agua en movimiento, hacer un montón de ramas, mantener a los gatos dentro durante la migración y proteger las ventanas y luces exteriores.

**Impacto** – Estas acciones ayudan a las aves cansadas a encontrar alimento, agua y refugio, aumentando sus posibilidades de sobrevivir. Por ejemplo, las plantas nativas dan alimento natural durante años, y el agua en movimiento atrae aves que no comen semillas. Mantener a los gatos dentro reduce el riesgo de que las aves sean cazadas.

**Próximo paso** – Las personas pueden comenzar plantando plantas nativas disponibles en viveros o instalando una fuente de agua simple esta semana. Con el tiempo, más jardines serán lugares seguros para las aves migratorias, lo que puede ayudar a mantener sus poblaciones.

**Resumen en una frase** – Cambios simples como plantar plantas nativas y ofrecer agua pueden convertir cualquier jardín en una parada vital para las aves migratorias este otoño.

articles.title: Tropical trees built homes for ants. Wasps are taking them over
articles.summary: Predatory wasps are hijacking shelters built by tropical trees for their ant defenders, potentially disrupting an ancient partnership that protects the plants from hungry insects. The takeover is far more common in disturbed landscapes such as oil palm plantations and could have lasting consequences for forest recovery and evolution.
articles.content:
Scientists studying the tropical forests of Malaysian Borneo have discovered an unexpected shift in one of the region's long-running ecological partnerships. An international team from Queen Mary University of London, the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, the Biology Center of the Czech Academy of Sciences, and other institutions found that predatory wasps are increasingly occupying the hollow stems of the tropical plant Macaranga pearsonii.

The findings, published in PeerJ, reveal that the wasps are moving into structures that evolved specifically to shelter protective ant colonies.

For at least 10 million years, these "ant-plants" have maintained a close partnership with ants. The plants produce hollow chambers where ants can live and also supply them with nutritious food bodies. In exchange, the ants aggressively protect their host plants from leaf-eating insects such as caterpillars.

Now, researchers have found evidence that this ancient relationship is being disrupted.

Predatory Wasps Take Over Ant Shelters

The team examined young Macaranga pearsonii trees growing in both logged forests and oil palm plantations. When researchers dissected the plants, they discovered that a species of predatory wasp was using the hollow chambers for an entirely different purpose.

Lead author Mr. Lestina explained:

"While surveying these ant-plants, I noticed that many stems had been hollowed out in an unusual way. When we opened them, they were full of flies being eaten alive by wasp larvae. Adult wasps hunt and paralyze the flies, then store them inside the plant's cavities as food for their young."

Rather than serving as homes for protective ants, some of the plant chambers had effectively become nurseries stocked with prey for developing wasp larvae.

The researchers also found a strong connection between wasp occupation and human-altered environments. Plants growing in oil palm plantations were much more likely to contain wasps than those found in logged forest.

Trees occupied by wasps also consistently had much smaller ant colonies. This pattern raises the possibility that the wasps are displacing the ants completely, although the researchers say experiments would be necessary to confirm whether that is actually happening.

Habitat Disturbance May Be Helping Wasps Spread

Co-author Dr. Kalsum M. Yusah explained:

"Human activities are transforming habitats worldwide, and this kind of shift in species interactions is exactly what we expect to see. We don't yet know whether this wasp is native or introduced, but its spread is clearly linked to disturbed landscapes."

The findings could have implications beyond the ants, wasps, and individual plants involved.

Macaranga species are often among the first plants to establish themselves in areas that have been cleared or damaged. If losing their ant defenders makes these plants less healthy, the effects could potentially influence the broader process of forest regeneration.

"If the plants lose their ant defenders and become less healthy, it could hinder forest recovery following disturbance," Dr. Yusah added.

An Ancient Partnership Could Change Over Time

Senior author Dr. Fayle from Queen Mary University of London said the disruption could eventually have evolutionary consequences.

"When mutualistic benefits break down, it can drive long-term evolutionary change. If these structures become less valuable to the plants because wasps exploit them, the plants may stop investing in them. These subtle, long-term consequences of human activity are far less understood than straightforward biodiversity loss."

The relationship between ants and these tropical plants represents just one of thousands of tightly connected ecological partnerships found in tropical ecosystems.

If human disturbance makes it easier for new "invaders" to enter these relationships, even when those species are native, other mutualistic partnerships could also become destabilized. That could weaken plants' natural defenses and alter which species become dominant within tropical forests.

The findings offer an early warning that ecological systems can begin changing in subtle ways long before species disappear entirely. In this case, the first sign is unfolding inside the hollow stems of tropical plants, where a partnership that has lasted millions of years may be starting to come apart.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant ecological discovery about how human disturbance is disrupting a long-standing mutualistic relationship between tropical trees and ants, with predatory wasps taking over ant shelters. This finding highlights the subtle but meaningful impacts of habitat disturbance on forest recovery and ecosystem evolution, offering important insights for conservation and environmental management.
articles.personality_title: Wasps are taking over homes built by tropical trees for protective ants
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In tropical forests of Malaysian Borneo, certain trees called Macaranga pearsonii have lived in partnership with ants for millions of years. The trees provide hollow spaces and food for ants, and in return, ants protect the trees from harmful insects.

**What happened** – Scientists found that predatory wasps are now moving into these hollow tree stems, using them as nurseries to raise their young by storing paralyzed flies as food. This takeover is most common in areas where forests have been disturbed by human activities, like oil palm plantations. Trees with wasps inside had fewer ants living in them.

**Impact** – This is important because the ants help keep the trees healthy by defending them. If wasps replace ants, the trees might become more vulnerable to insect damage. Since these trees often grow first in damaged areas, losing their ant defenders could slow down forest recovery. It also shows how human changes to the environment can quietly disrupt long-lasting natural partnerships.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to study if wasps are completely pushing ants out and how this change might affect forest growth over time. Understanding this can help guide efforts to protect forests and keep these natural relationships strong.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Human disturbance is allowing wasps to take over homes built by tropical trees for ants, which could affect forest health and recovery.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les guêpes envahissent les maisons construites par les arbres tropicaux pour les fourmis protectrices
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Dans les forêts tropicales du Bornéo malaisien, certains arbres appelés Macaranga pearsonii vivent en partenariat avec des fourmis depuis des millions d’années. Les arbres offrent des cavités et de la nourriture aux fourmis, qui en échange protègent les arbres contre les insectes nuisibles.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques ont découvert que des guêpes prédatrices s’installent maintenant dans ces cavités, les utilisant comme nurseries pour élever leurs larves en stockant des mouches paralysées comme nourriture. Cette invasion est surtout fréquente dans les zones où la forêt a été perturbée par l’homme, comme les plantations de palmier à huile. Les arbres occupés par des guêpes avaient moins de fourmis.

**Impact** – Cela est important car les fourmis aident à garder les arbres en bonne santé en les défendant. Si les guêpes remplacent les fourmis, les arbres pourraient être plus vulnérables aux dégâts d’insectes. Ces arbres poussent souvent en premier dans les zones endommagées, donc perdre leurs fourmis protectrices pourrait ralentir la récupération de la forêt. Cela montre aussi comment les activités humaines peuvent perturber discrètement des partenariats naturels anciens.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent étudier si les guêpes chassent complètement les fourmis et comment ce changement pourrait affecter la croissance des forêts à long terme. Comprendre cela peut aider à mieux protéger les forêts et à maintenir ces relations naturelles.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les perturbations humaines permettent aux guêpes de prendre la place des fourmis dans les arbres tropicaux, ce qui pourrait nuire à la santé et à la récupération des forêts.
articles.personality_title_es: Avispas ocupan hogares construidos por árboles tropicales para hormigas protectoras
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En los bosques tropicales de Borneo malayo, ciertos árboles llamados Macaranga pearsonii han vivido en asociación con hormigas durante millones de años. Los árboles les ofrecen espacios huecos y alimento, y a cambio, las hormigas protegen a los árboles de insectos dañinos.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos descubrieron que avispas depredadoras están ocupando estos tallos huecos, usándolos como guarderías para sus crías al almacenar moscas paralizadas como alimento. Esta ocupación es más común en áreas donde los bosques han sido alterados por actividades humanas, como las plantaciones de palma aceitera. Los árboles con avispas tenían menos hormigas.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque las hormigas ayudan a mantener los árboles sanos al protegerlos. Si las avispas reemplazan a las hormigas, los árboles podrían ser más vulnerables a daños. Como estos árboles suelen crecer primero en áreas dañadas, perder a las hormigas defensoras podría retrasar la recuperación del bosque. También muestra cómo los cambios humanos pueden alterar silenciosamente asociaciones naturales antiguas.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren estudiar si las avispas están desplazando totalmente a las hormigas y cómo este cambio podría afectar el crecimiento del bosque a largo plazo. Entender esto puede ayudar a proteger mejor los bosques y mantener estas relaciones naturales.

**Resumen en una frase** – La alteración humana permite que avispas ocupen los hogares que los árboles tropicales construyeron para hormigas, lo que podría afectar la salud y recuperación del bosque.
articles.image_prompt: A detailed, warm-toned painting of a hollow tropical Macaranga pearsonii stem split open to reveal two contrasting chambers side by side: one filled with protective ants tending the plant and nurturing it, and the other occupied by predatory wasps with larvae feeding on paralyzed flies, symbolizing an ancient partnership disrupted by wasps taking over the ants’ homes, all rendered in soft natural greens, browns, and muted yellows.
